title: Rapiscan and Taronga/Macquarie 3D X-ray CT algorithms auto-detect dried shark fins, seahorses and sea cucumbers at 86–96% in a proof of concept; no customs deployment
summary: Pirotta et al. (2026) trained 3D CNN algorithms on 298 CT scans: detection 95% shark fin, 96% seahorse, 86% sea cucumber with low false alarms; authors say front-line implementation is the next step.
account: Pirotta et al., in Frontiers in Ocean Sustainability (published 8 June 2026), used Rapiscan 3D X-ray computed tomography (CT) technology to build AI algorithms. The algorithms autodetect marine wildlife in mail and air-traveler pathways. The work used 298 scans from 68 samples of dried shark fin, seahorse and sea cucumber. It expanded them with 3D convolutional neural networks and 3D Threat Image Projection. Detection rates were 95% (shark fin), 96% (seahorse) and 86% (sea cucumber), with false alarm rates of 2%, 9% and 1%. The authors include Rapiscan Systems staff and researchers at Taronga Conservation Society, Macquarie University, NSW DPIRD, the Australian Museum and others. They state that the paper “demonstrates the efficacy and potential impact of AI detection tools to complement existing methods”. In The Conversation (7 June 2026) the lead authors reported success rates of 95%, 95% and 85%. They wrote that “The next step is relying on implementation of these algorithms at the front lines”. Earth.Org (21 May 2026), which is not among the sources, reported that the tool is a proof of concept with no operational customs use. That check also found that a Buenos Aires seizure it mentioned did not involve the tool.
purpose: Automated detection of trafficked marine wildlife in 3D X-ray screening of mail and luggage to support customs inspection; no operational use yet.
